catalog_quote: A phonological word in Dadibi consists of one obligatory nuclear syllable with a high or low tone and from zero to 6 marginal syllables. 3.1 Description When the nuclear syllable of the word is high tone, it has extra intensity (sometimes very slight). High nuclear tones tend to pull following pitches to high and the words have a very quick tempo. When a low tone falls on the nuclear syllable, it has extra length. Low nuclear syllables tend to pull following pitches toward low, and the words are much slower in tempo. Preceding syllables tend to fluctuate. ... The contrastive intensity of the nuclear syllable seems to be of more importance than the correct tone on that syllable. However, by knowing the correct nuclear tone one is able to determine the appropriate tempo, the overall pitch and rhythm ... 3.2.2 Two syllable words: High on the first syllable contrasts with high on the second…

new_statements.rule_in_words: The suprasegmental section names tone, stress and length but only describes tone: two contrastive tones, high and low, illustrated with minimal pairs on monosyllables (wà/wá) and on disyllables where the tone-marked syllable is either the first (káli, àga) or the second (kalí, kebá, kebà, agà). Nothing is said about stress placement. (Also: 'Nasalization is contrastive on all five vowels', p. 2; 'Phonemic tone is not written' in the orthography, p. 3.)
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Dadibi (Mikaru) [mps] of Karimui District, Chimbu Province, PNG, as documented by SIL (G. and G. MacDonald); no dialect is singled out. The OPD lists Noru, Masi, Kalabai, Negabo, Nornai as major villages.

new_statements.quote: The tonal pattern of Dadibi (MacDonald and MacDonald 1974; Trans-New Guinea) also follows the same general pattern: there is only one syllable on the word which bears contrastive tone, and this may be called the stressed syllable (MacDonald and MacDonald label it the “nuclear syllable”). A constellation of effects accompany a High or Low tone on such a nuclear syllable. A High tone has extra intensity, tends to raise the pitch of following tones, and the tempo of the word is faster. A Low tone lengthens the nuclear syllable, tends to lower the pitch of following syllables, and slows the tempo of the entire word. Tones preceding the nuclear syllable tend to fluctuate in pitch.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog rule is empty; this is the first stress statement for Dadibi in our check. It gives the prosodic type (word tone anchored on one stressed/nuclear syllable per word, H vs L contrast on that syllable) and shows that the stressed syllable's position is lexically variable, not fixed. Compatible with the 1992 OPD (two tones, tone-marked syllable in varying position). The primary source is MacDonald & MacDonald 1974 'Dadibi Phonology' (Workpapers in PNG Languages 4), which should be quoted directly if it is obtainable.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Dadibi is a word-tone language of the 'one nuclear syllable' type (Cahill groups it with Fasu, Kairi and Awad Bing): each word has exactly one nuclear syllable, which is the stressed syllable and the only syllable bearing a contrastive tone (H or L); the other syllables are unspecified for tone and take their pitch from the environment. The position of the nuclear/stressed syllable is not fixed: Cahill's ex. (7) on p. 8 shows it on the first or second syllable of disyllables (káli 'kaukau' vs kalí 'tree type'; píni 'bird type' vs piní 'small bat'; kebá 'axe' vs kebà 'canoe') and on the first, second or third syllable of trisyllables (bílibo 'moving', bìdibo 'staying'; silága 'bush food', medàbu 'bone needle'; masalú 'scar', hanamù 'soot'), so stress location is lexical. Cahill explicitly says this variable location 'is reminiscent of a pitch accent system, but it does not fit the usual pitch accent type, since the accented syllable may itself exhibit contrastive tone' (p. 7, said of Fasu and extended to Dadibi as 'the same general pattern'). Suffixes/clitics contribute their own tone (ex. 8).
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; the account is second-hand (Cahill summarising MacDonald & MacDonald 1974)

audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim at the stated pages in the SIL scan we hold (scanned + page scan). The deciding source is the dedicated primary phonology (MacDonald & MacDonald 1974), which is the best and essentially only description of Dadibi prosody; Glottolog lists no competing phonology and web search found no later instrumental/phonological work. Two open items downloaded now — MacDonald's 1992 Organised Phonology Data (primary, same minimal pairs, two contrastive tones on one syllable per word) and Cahill 2011 (secondary survey explicitly equating the nuclear tone-bearing syllable with stress, position lexically contrastive) — both confirm the 'tonal (culminative word-tone), no independent positional stress rule' coding. Only unheld descriptive work is the 1976 UPNG MA grammar (print only), unlikely to change anything.
